This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 45-1011.00 “First-Line Supervisors of Farming, Fishing, and Forestry Workers” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation, and the body text follows that official occupational scope). Even within farming, forestry, and fishing on-site supervision, the differences are large: field crop cultivation, orchards and nurseries and greenhouses, livestock and poultry farming, aquaculture and fishing, forestry and logging operations, and agricultural machinery and irrigation facility management; a supervisor may lead only one work crew or simultaneously arrange several plots and several work sites. Before comparing positions or development paths, first check: the education and experience required for the role, whether specialty qualifications such as agricultural machinery operation or plant protection and chemical application are required, agricultural and forestry work safety and machinery protection training requirements, working hours and seasonal arrangements (including long hours during the busy farming season), and whether production planning and cost management responsibility is required.

Validate with one paper exercise: you are given a completely fictitious farming or forestry work assignment (type and scale of the plot, forest land, or aquaculture site, the work items to be completed this season, available personnel and machinery, supplies and feed or chemical inventory, the weather and farming-season window, an equipment failure or safety violation incident, and the records and reporting to be completed). You are asked to write out the shift work assignments and scheduling, the work sequence and quality standards, safety and protection key points, supply and machinery dispatch, the incident handling and escalation path, and the records and reports to be used, and to mark which decisions must be made by the production lead or personnel with specialty qualifications.

Signals worth considering more: willingness to work outdoors and at field, forest, or aquaculture sites over the long term, ability to arrange work according to the farming season and weather, and willingness to manage workers according to safety procedures. Signals requiring caution: unwillingness to work outdoors in physically demanding environments over the long term, difficulty enduring long working hours during the busy farming season, and imagining farming and forestry work as only sitting in a mechanized cab.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute hiring, ability scoring, safety, or compliance conclusions.

First judge whether you are willing to make the organization and supervision of farming, forestry, and fishing field work a long-term career: it requires working outdoors over the long term, arranging production according to the farming season and weather, organizing work crews and supervising machinery and chemical safety, and bearing supervisory responsibility for the safety of workers, livestock, and equipment; validate with the paper exercise and seven-day task on this page.

The work of first-line supervisors of farming, fishing, and forestry workers revolves around the cycle of “work preparation—assignment and scheduling—on-site patrol and progress control—safety and equipment and supply management—records and review”: before work, check the work plan and plot, forest land, or aquaculture site conditions, check that personnel, machinery, and supplies are in place, and complete the safety briefing; assign work and schedule shifts according to the work plan, specify the work sequence, quality standards, and safety requirements, and teach operating methods to workers; during work, patrol fields, forest land, aquaculture facilities, and work faces to judge conditions and progress, check crop, livestock, and fish conditions, and promptly handle and report pests, diseases, or anomalies; supervise compliance with safety procedures and warn or discipline violators according to rules; requisition feed, chemicals, equipment, and parts and dispatch machinery; record output, personnel, and equipment conditions as well as pay and personnel matters, assist with equipment adjustment and repair, and take part in production plan and budget discussions. The emphasis differs greatly by direction: the field and orchard direction stresses the farming season and plant protection, the nursery and greenhouse direction stresses environmental control and quality, the livestock and poultry direction stresses feeding and disease prevention, the aquaculture direction stresses water quality and feeding, and the forestry and logging direction stresses operational safety and volume management.
U.S. O*NET-SOC 45-1011.00 “First-Line Supervisors of Farming, Fishing, and Forestry Workers”: directly supervise and coordinate the work of agricultural, forestry, aquaculture, and related workers.

Work context | First-line supervisors of farming, fishing, and forestry workers focus on organizing outdoor field work, and workload is clearly affected by the farming season and weather. O*NET work context shows that work schedules are mostly regular (63% regular), with 34% irregular; among weekly work hours, 66% exceed 40 hours and 34% are 40 hours; 55% maintain continuous contact with others and 31% contact most of the time; 82% have face-to-face discussions every day; 69% have telephone conversations every day and 25% once a week or more; 70% consider the work to require extremely precise or highly accurate work combined (30% extremely important, 40% very important); the consequences of error are extremely serious for 34%, very serious for 15%, and serious for 23%; 40% have strict deadlines every day; conflict situations occur once a week or more for 29% and never for 16%; 39% have very high responsibility for the health and safety of others and 33% high responsibility; 65% must make decisions every day; 52% rate collaboration with the work crew or team as extremely important and 25% very important; 30% rate coordinating or leading others as extremely important and 25% very important; the degree of automation of the work is 26% moderately automated, 36% slightly automated, and 28% not at all automated; 71% work outdoors in all weather every day; 31% are exposed to extreme heat or cold every day and 33% once a week or more; 41% are exposed to contaminants every day; 29% are exposed to hazardous equipment every day; 24% are exposed to minor burns, cuts, or bites every day; 21% are exposed to noise every day.

Main objects | Work crew personnel and temporary workers, crops and timber and livestock and farmed fish, farmland and forest land and aquaculture facilities, agricultural machinery and irrigation equipment, feed and chemicals and equipment supplies, and output and personnel records.

Collaboration | Collaboration with the production lead or farm owner, veterinarians and plant protection and aquaculture technical personnel, agricultural machinery repairers, supply and feed vendors, buyers and transporters, and adjacent work crews.

Tools and materials | Tractors and harvesting machinery, irrigation and fertilization equipment, plant protection and chemical application implements, feeding and feeding equipment, measuring and testing instruments, scheduling and inventory management software, and output and pay record forms.

Institutional basis | Agricultural and forestry safety production requirements, pesticide and veterinary drug use management rules, machinery and equipment operation and protection requirements, animal welfare and disease prevention requirements, and employment and pay record rules.

Record requirements | Work and assignment records, chemical and feed and supply use records, machinery inspection and repair records, output and quality records, and personnel and pay and personnel records must be kept on file according to institutional rules.

Practice boundaries | Matters involving pesticide and veterinary drug use, disease prevention, machinery structural and electrical repair, and agricultural product quality safety must be handled by personnel or professional bodies with the corresponding qualifications according to procedures; this page does not provide specific advice on plant protection, veterinary care, machinery repair, or safe operation.

Environment and pace | Work is mainly outdoors, driven by weather and the farming season, and the busy farming season concentrates work intensity and requires long hours; the site involves machinery injury, pesticide and veterinary drug exposure, livestock and fish work, and high and low temperature risks.

Region and scope | U.S. O*NET-SOC 45-1011.00 does not map one-to-one onto mainland China's occupational classification; the mainland's agricultural machinery operation qualifications, pesticide and veterinary drug use, animal disease prevention, and forestry logging safety requirements must be verified separately according to local and competent department regulations.

entries.answer: This page is written according to U.S. O*NET-SOC 45-1011.00 'First-Line Supervisors of Farming, Fishing, and Forestry Workers' (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation, and the body text follows that official occupational scope): directly supervise and coordinate the work of workers in agriculture, forestry, aquaculture, and related operations. Specifically: before work, check the work plan and work area conditions, confirm that personnel, machinery, and materials are in place, and complete the safety briefing; assign work and schedule shifts according to the work plan, clarify work sequence and quality standards, and teach operating methods to workers; patrol fields, woodlands, farming facilities, and the work area to judge work conditions and progress, check the condition of crops, livestock, and fish, and handle anomalies; supervise compliance with safety procedures and machinery guards and issue warnings or handle violations according to the rules; requisition feed, pesticides, implements, and parts and dispatch machinery; record output, personnel, and equipment conditions as well as pay and personnel matters; and assist with equipment adjustment and repair and take part in production planning and cost discussions.
entries.question: What do First-Line Supervisors of Farming, Fishing, and Forestry Workers mainly do?

entries.answer: The scope of management and the outputs differ: this occupation's main outputs are work crew assignment and scheduling, farming-calendar progress, and safety supervision, making it a frontline management position; Agricultural Workers and other farmworkers produce by directly performing crop and livestock production and harvesting work; Farmers, Ranchers, and Other Agricultural Managers focus on business decisions, production planning, and cost budgeting, with a larger management scope; Forest and Conservation Workers produce afforestation, tending, and patrol work; Hunting and Fishing Workers produce catching and farming work; Logging Equipment Operators produce felling and skidding machinery work; Agricultural Inspectors focus on inspecting and issuing reports in accordance with the law; and First-Line Supervisors of Production and Operating Workers produce crew management on processing and manufacturing sites.

subject.name: First-Line Supervisors of Farming, Fishing, and Forestry Workers
subject.summary: Directly supervise and coordinate the work of agricultural, forestry, aquaculture, and related workers: includes assigning work and scheduling shifts, arranging planting and harvesting or breeding and harvesting according to work plans, teaching operating methods and safety procedures to workers, patrolling fields, forest land, and aquaculture facilities to judge working conditions and progress, supervising compliance with safety procedures and correcting violations, requisitioning feed, chemicals, and equipment and supplies, recording output and personnel and equipment conditions, and assisting with equipment adjustment and repair.
